stem:
A 10-year-old boy was hit on the nose by a cricket ball 3 hours ago. His nose is swollen and slightly deviated, and both nostrils now feel blocked. Anterior rhinoscopy shows a smooth, purplish swelling on both sides of the nasal septum that indents softly when pressed with a cotton bud. His airway and observations are stable.

What is the most appropriate next step for the emergency doctor?

options.label: A
options.text: Nasal X-ray, then fracture clinic review in 5–7 days
options.explanation: Nasal fractures are reassessed at 5–7 days once swelling settles, and X-rays add little; a septal haematoma cannot wait that long.

options.label: B
options.text: Same-day ENT referral for drainage of the swelling
options.explanation: Correct. Soft, compressible swelling on both sides of the septum after nasal trauma is a septal haematoma. It needs same-day ENT drainage to prevent septal abscess, cartilage necrosis and saddle-nose deformity.

options.label: C
options.text: Ice and analgesia, with GP review in 3–5 days
options.explanation: Waiting days risks infection and loss of septal cartilage.

options.label: D
options.text: Topical decongestant and review once swelling settles
options.explanation: A decongestant shrinks mucosa but does not drain blood trapped under the perichondrium.

options.label: E
options.text: Anterior nasal packing to reduce the swelling
options.explanation: Packing alone, without incision and drainage, leaves the haematoma in place.

context: After nasal trauma, a fluctuant septal swelling is a septal haematoma until proven otherwise. It requires same-day ENT assessment and drainage.
